01 — Why it matters

A worn or mismatched nozzle quietly decides your FUJI yield

Nobody orders a NXT because of its nozzles — but the nozzle is the only thing that actually touches your component. Its tip diameter sets whether a 0402 lifts square; its matrix code sets whether the head even recognises it; its material sets how fast it wears. On a high-mix EMS line running FUJI, the nozzle is where mispicks, skewed parts, tombstoning and 'mystery' reject spikes really come from. Southern Machinery makes the nozzle the predictable part.

01

The tip sets the pick

A NXT head does not pick a component; it picks a position through a tip. When the tip is wrong for the part — too wide, too narrow, the wrong material — the head reaches, misses the centre of gravity, and the placement is marginal. Every mispick traces back to a tip that was never matched to the part.

02

The matrix code is not decoration

FUJI nozzles carry an OEM data-matrix and colour-matrix code so the machine knows exactly which tip is in which position. A replacement without the correct codes can be mis-read, rejected, or silently used at the wrong speed — the reject rate climbs and nobody knows why. We reproduce the codes.

03

OEM pricing squeezes the spares budget

Genuine FUJI nozzles are expensive and often carry long lead times, so factories run them past their useful life to avoid a stop. That is a false economy: one stopped NXT head costs more in an hour than a whole set of matched nozzles. A traceable aftermarket source turns the spares line from a hostage into a plan.

02 — The method

From your head to a fitted nozzle in six documented moves

Nozzle supply is not catalogue roulette. It is a matching discipline: read the machine and head, cross-reference the part number and matrix code, choose the geometry and material for the actual component, then verify dimensions before it ever reaches your line. This is the sequence Southern Machinery engineers follow on every FUJI order, and the same one we invite you to run against your own part master.

01

Read the machine and head

Everything starts with the model and head — NXT H01, H04, H04S, H08, H12, H08M or H24, or a CP4 / CP6 / QP / IP-3 / XP inserter, or a GL dispenser head. The head fixes the shank, the holder interface and the vacuum take-off, so it is the first fact we record.

02

Cross-reference the part number and code

We match your nozzle against the FUJI taxonomy — the FU-AAxxxxx NXT nozzle series and the CP/QP/IP nozzle assemblies — and reproduce the OEM data-matrix and colour-matrix identification so the head reads the replacement natively.

03

Choose the tip geometry

The component decides the tip: a 0201 or 0402 needs the ø0.3–ø0.7 micro-tip, a MELF needs a dedicated MELF bore, a large IC or electrolytic needs a wide ø5.0–ø15.0 tip or a gripper, and an LED or odd-form part may need a custom profile.

04

Select material and pad

Ceramic for fine-pitch, low-static, long-life picking; metal for rugged larger parts; rubber-pad (G) tips for sensitive bodies where a hard tip would mark or crack. The document lists the G (rubber pad) and MELF variants against real part numbers.

05

Manufacture and dimensionally verify

Each nozzle is ground to the OEM dimensions and checked — tip diameter, bore, concentricity, matrix code, shank fit — before it ships. The pick position must be identical on cycle one and cycle five hundred thousand.

06

Drop in and confirm the first pick

Because the fit is dimensional to the head holder and the code matches, the nozzle drops in and is recognised without re-teaching. We ask for a first-article pick on your own tape so the match is proven on your line, not just on the drawing.

Machine families, head models, tip diameters, materials and the matrix-code identification are quoted from the Southern Machinery Fuji Nozzles & Consumables document and the FUJI NXT head reference.

How the nozzle is built to pick

Ceramic fine-pitch tips

Low static, hard and wear-resistant — the choice for 0201, 0402 and 0603 chips where the pick centre must not drift.

Metal & MELF tips

Rugged tips and dedicated MELF bores for larger chips and glass-bodied MELF that a fine tip would drop or crack.

Rubber-pad (G) tips

The document's G variants add a rubber pad for sensitive bodies that a hard tip would mark — a gentle grip on LEDs and delicate parts.

Reproduced matrix codes

OEM data-matrix and colour-matrix identification is reproduced so the FUJI head recognises the nozzle and its position natively.

Ground concentricity

The tip is ground to the OEM dimensions so the pick position stays the same on cycle one and cycle five hundred thousand.

Clean vacuum channel

Bore and channel integrity keep suction stable and resist the clogging that turns into intermittent mispicks.

06 — Fitting & ordering

How to order a nozzle that fits first time

Getting a matched FUJI nozzle is a short, repeatable process. Here is the sequence we run with every new EMS customer, so the part arrives ready to drop into the head and be recognised.

Identify the machine and head

Note the model (NXT, CP, QP, IP, XP, AX or GL) and the head — H01, H04, H04S, H08, H12, H08M or H24. A photo of the head and the existing nozzle is enough to start.

Give us the part number

Send the FUJI nozzle P/N (the FU-AAxxxxx NXT series or the CP/QP/IP assembly code) printed on the nozzle or in your spares list.

Confirm geometry, material & code

We check the tip diameter, bore, MELF/G variant and matrix code against the component you place, and flag anything to change for your wear pattern.

Sample & dimensional verify

For new or custom tips we ship a sample and confirm tip diameter, bore, concentricity, matrix code and shank fit against the drawing.

Fit to the head

Drop-in fit to the holder and recognised by the head — no re-teaching. Run a first-article pick on your own tape to confirm the match.

Maintain & schedule swaps

Track cycle counts, change the head filters, clean the vacuum channel, and reorder from a named part number before the tip drifts into a reject.

ARTICLE 01The one millimetre nobody specs — and why it decides your yield

The nozzle is the only thing in the pick-and-place cycle that touches the component, yet it rarely appears on the machine spec sheet.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

Every SMT engineer can name the FUJI NXT that placed a part. Almost none can name the nozzle that picked it. That is the gap: the nozzle is the single component in the whole pick-and-place cycle that physically touches your board, and it is the one nobody specs.

Think about the last 'mystery' reject spike you chased on the NXT. You looked at the program, the feeder, the calibration, the head. You probably did not look at the tip — because it looked fine, and because it never occurred to you that a few microns of tip wear could move the pick centre off the component's centre of gravity. That is exactly what it does. The head reaches for a position; the tip decides whether the part actually sits where the head expects.

The reusable method is to treat the nozzle as a spec'd part of the process, not a consumable you replace when it visibly breaks. Three questions on your changeover card: what is the tip diameter and material for this part, which NXT head does it sit in, and how many cycles has this tip run? If you cannot answer all three, you are running a component you have not specified.

Southern Machinery's FUJI nozzle range is built around that discipline: a documented tip window from the ø0.3 micro-tip up to the ø15.0 large-component nozzle, mapped across the NXT H01, H04, H04S, H08, H12, H08M and H24 heads and the CP/QP/IP inserters, in ceramic, metal and rubber-pad materials. The tip is the product; the rest is the head.

Once the nozzle is on the card, the second-order effect shows up over a quarter: the pick centre stops drifting, the reject rate stops having a personality, and the conversation with the operator changes from 'what did you touch' to 'when do we swap'. The parts stay the same. The behaviour of the line changes.

Send us your machine model, head and the part number printed on the nozzle — or just a clear photo of the tip. We will match it against the FUJI taxonomy and tell you, honestly, whether a standard tip fixes your problem or whether you need a custom geometry. info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576.

ARTICLE 02Why the matrix code on a FUJI nozzle is not decoration

The data-matrix and colour-matrix code tells the head which tip is where — and what happens when a replacement does not carry it.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

Flip over a genuine FUJI NXT nozzle and you will see two small codes on the flange — a data-matrix and a colour-matrix. They look like decoration. They are not. They are how the machine knows exactly which tip is sitting in which position.

Here is the failure nobody logs: a factory fits a replacement nozzle that picks perfectly on the bench but carries the wrong — or no — matrix code. The head reads it as a different tip, applies the wrong pick height or speed, or flags a mismatch. On a single part it is invisible; across a shift it is a rising reject rate blamed on the feeder, the tape, the program — anything but the code on the nozzle.

The reusable method is to treat the code as part of the spec, not an accessory. When you replace a nozzle, verify three things: the tip diameter matches the part, the shank matches the head, and the matrix and colour codes match what the machine expects for that position. If a supplier cannot reproduce the codes, they are selling you a pick that the head cannot trust.

This is why Southern Machinery reproduces the OEM data-matrix and colour-matrix identification on its FUJI nozzles. The document records the tip diameters, the MELF and rubber-pad (G) variants and the FU-AAxxxx part-number format across the H01 to H24 heads; we match the geometry and the code together, so the head recognises the nozzle natively and the pick height is right on the first placement.

Add the matrix code to your nozzle changeover checklist next to the part number. The first time a 'good' nozzle causes a bad shift, you will already know to check the code before you tear into the program.

Send us the head model and a photo of your current nozzle flange. We will confirm the tip, the shank and the codes, and quote a matched replacement the head will read without a second thought.

ARTICLE 03ø0.3 to ø15 mm — choosing the tip for the part

A method for reading your component and matching it to the right NXT head and tip diameter.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

A FUJI NXT head can take tips from ø0.3 all the way to ø15.0. That range is the whole point of the machine — and the whole trap. Pick the wrong diameter and you either crush a 0402 or fail to lift a large electrolytic.

The method is to choose the tip from the component, then confirm the head, not the other way round. A 0201 or 0402 wants the fine ø0.3–ø0.7 tip on an H08 or H08M head, where a wider tip would disturb the neighbouring pads. A MELF wants a dedicated MELF bore — the document lists ø1.3M, ø1.8M, ø2.5M variants — because a standard tip grips a glass body unevenly. A large IC or QFP wants the ø5.0–ø15.0 tip on an H04 or H01. A sensitive LED or delicate body wants a rubber-pad (G) tip so a hard surface never marks it.

Read your part master this way and the tip stops being a guess. For each high-volume component, note the package, the body size and the head it is placed on; that triple points to one tip diameter and one material. The FUJI taxonomy in the Southern Machinery document maps exactly those combinations across the H01, H04, H04S, H08, H12, H08M and H24 heads.

Once the tip is chosen by the part, the failure modes stop surprising you. The 0402 stops tombstoning because the fine tip lifts it square; the MELF stops cracking because the MELF bore holds it evenly; the LED stops marking because the rubber-pad tip never touches it hard. The part did not change. The tip did.

Keep a small set of the common diameters and the MELF and G variants on the shelf with the parts they belong to, and flag them on the changeover card so the next engineer reaches for the right tip instead of the generic one.

Tell us what you place — the package, the body and the head — and we will recommend the tip diameter and material, and ship samples of the two or three worth testing, with the reasoning written down.

ARTICLE 04The part number you cannot read

How to identify a worn FUJI nozzle and turn an illegible marking into an exact replacement.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

Half the nozzle orders we get start with a photo of a part number that has worn off. The marking is tiny, it sits on a curved body, and after a few hundred thousand picks it is simply gone. The factory knows it has a FU-AAxxxx on the head; it cannot read which one.

The method for turning an illegible nozzle into an exact replacement is three facts and one picture. Fact one: the machine and head — NXT H01, H04, H04S, H08, H12, H08M or H24, or a CP/QP/IP inserter. Fact two: the head position. Fact three: the component you place there. The picture: the tip, straight on and from the side, next to a coin for scale, plus a shot of the flange so we can see the matrix and colour codes. With those, the FUJI taxonomy does the rest — the head narrows the series, the component narrows the tip, and the photo confirms the geometry and code.

This is why Southern Machinery keeps the full compatibility mapping rather than a price list. The document records the FU-AAxxxx NXT series by head and the CP/QP/IP assembly codes with their tip diameters and MELF/G variants, so an unreadable marking becomes a lookup on the machine, not on the ink.

Once identified, the replacement carries the same identity your program expects: same series, same bore, same material, same matrix and colour codes, dimensionally matched to the holder. The part number you could not read is now a named line on your spares shelf, and the next swap does not start with a photo shoot.

Put a small label of the machine model and head position on your spares register, not just the P/N — because the P/N is the thing that wears off and the model is the thing that does not.

Send us the photo and the three facts. We will identify the series, confirm the tip and codes against the component, and quote a matched replacement with a one-day spare-parts lead time on the standard family.

ARTICLE 05Running a nozzle past its life is a false economy

The real cost of stretching a tip, measured against the hour of head time it eventually costs you.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

The most expensive nozzle is the one you keep too long. Running a tip past its life saves a purchase order and costs you an hour of head time — usually at the worst possible moment.

The arithmetic is simple and most factories refuse to do it. A high-speed FUJI NXT head is a six-figure-per-hour asset. A worn nozzle does not announce itself; it shows up as a rising reject rate, a skewed part that passes inspection and fails at reflow, and the occasional stopped head mid-shift. One stopped head for an hour costs more than a full set of matched nozzles for the machine. Stretching the spares budget to avoid a small purchase is a false economy that hides inside the 'consumables' line.

The method is to swap on evidence, not on failure. Track the cycle count per tip, change the head filters on schedule, clean the vacuum channel, and set a swap interval from the wear you actually see — the reject rate and the CPK, not the calendar. Keep named-part-number spares on the shelf so a scheduled swap is a morning's work.

This is exactly what the one-day spare-parts lead time and the single-piece-to-batch MOQ are for. You do not need to hoard nozzles to avoid running a worn tip; you need a traceable source that ships the right part number fast, and the filters and consumables to stretch the useful life honestly. Both are in the document, not in a promise.

Put the swap interval and the filter change on the maintenance plan next to the nozzle part number. The tip that fails silently is the one you never scheduled — so schedule it.

Want the shelf inventory? Send us your head count and daily volumes. We will turn the named part numbers into a spares kit with quantities and a filter/consumables plan, and quote it with the nozzles.

ARTICLE 06LEDs and odd-form parts need odd-form tips

Rubber-pad, gripper and custom geometries — matching shape to the parts that defeat a standard tip.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

Ask an operator which parts are hardest to place on a FUJI and they will not name the 0402. They will name the LED, the connector, the odd-shaped thing that a standard vacuum tip keeps dropping, marking or skewing.

Odd-form parts defeat a round tip for a physical reason: there is no flat, clean surface for vacuum to grab, the body is too delicate for a hard tip, or the part must be held by a lead a suction cup cannot seat on. The answer is geometry and material, not force. A rubber-pad (G) tip grips an LED or a sensitive body without marking it. A dedicated MELF bore holds a glass-bodied part evenly. A mechanical gripper grabs a terminal or connector by the lead when vacuum cannot hold it at all. And when nothing in the catalog fits, a custom tip is designed.

The Southern Machinery document lists these variants against real FUJI part numbers — the G rubber-pad tips across the NXT heads, the MELF bores at ø1.3M, ø1.8M and ø2.5M, and the custom and LED nozzle path for special applications — so odd-form picking is a documented route, not an experiment.

Once you match geometry and material to the part, the awkward ones stop being the line's weak point. The LED that used to mark is held by a rubber-pad tip; the MELF that used to crack is held by a MELF bore; the terminal that used to drop is held by a gripper. The part did not change. The tip did.

Keep a small set of the G, MELF and gripper variants on the shelf with the parts they belong to, and flag them on the changeover card so the next engineer reaches for the right shape instead of the generic one.

Have a part that keeps dropping, marking or skewing? Send a photo of the component and the board. We will tell you whether a rubber-pad, MELF, gripper or custom tip is the answer, and what it costs.

ARTICLE 07You do not need a drawing to get a custom nozzle

The three photographs and two numbers that start a five-day nozzle design.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

The scariest sentence in nozzle supply is 'our part is special, there is no tip for it'. The least scary version of it is a photograph.

Every custom project stalls at the same place: the customer is asked for a drawing and does not have one — because the part is a locally-sourced LED, a custom connector, a component with no CAD. The truth our engineering desk has learned over fifteen years of spare parts: a custom nozzle design does not need a drawing. It needs to see the part, and to know how many you place.

Here is the three-photo method. Photo one: the component out of the package, next to a coin — that gives us the body and the tip size, from the ø0.3 micro-tip up to the ø15.0 large-component nozzle, or tells us it is outside the window. Photo two: the part from the side and from the pick face, so we can see whether it needs a bore, a rubber pad, a MELF tip or a gripper that closes on a lead. Photo three: the board, so we can see spacing and neighbours and know which head the tip must fit. Then two numbers: the machine and head, and your daily volume.

With five inputs, the documented five-day design service returns a nozzle concept — geometry, bore, material, matrix code and the shank interface to your head — not a brochure. The custom and LED nozzle path is the documented path across the whole range: the same document that lists the standard NXT series is the one we extend when no catalog tip fits.

Design cycles shrink when the evidence arrives early. The project that starts with three photos finishes with a first-article pick on your own tape; the project that starts with a request for a drawing finishes in a shared drive.

Take the three photos today and send them to info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576. We will tell you within one working day whether your special part is a catalog tip or a five-day custom design — and what each one costs.

ARTICLE 08A nozzle budget you can actually defend

Four honest lines that turn spares from a grudge purchase into a plan.

Article body shown in English; summaries localised.

Most nozzle quotations are dishonest in the same direction: the vendor's sheet shows a saving you will never collect. Here is the opposite method — four lines, your numbers, and a bias toward under-claiming.

Line one: how many nozzles do you actually replace in a year, and what do you pay for each today? Not the brochure figure — the invoices. Line two: what would a matched, matrix-coded aftermarket nozzle cost, and what share of that spend could you realistically switch? Be honest; some heads you will keep genuine. Line three: what does an hour of stopped NXT head time cost you, and how many changeover hours and working days does a good nozzle source save you per year? Line four: add the purchase saving to the downtime you avoid. That total is your real number, and every figure in it is one you typed.

The calculator on this page runs exactly those four lines, with nothing pre-baked. No invented time studies, no competitor-bashing multipliers, no price hard-coded anywhere — the OEM price and our price are both boxes you fill in. The defaults are placeholders for the arithmetic, not claims about your factory.

Now the savings the method deliberately leaves out, because they are yours to prove: the tombstoned and skewed parts a worn tip lets through, the rework and scrap those cause, and the reject spikes a drifting nozzle hides until they arrive at reflow. Those are real, and they are bigger than the purchase price — but we will not put a fake number on them.

FAQ

Questions EMS buyers ask before ordering

Do these fit genuine FUJI NXT heads?
Yes. We match the shank and holder interface dimensionally to the OEM nozzle for the head you run — NXT H01, H04, H04S, H08, H12, H08M and H24, plus CP, QP, IP and XP inserters — and reproduce the data-matrix and colour-matrix identification so the head recognises the nozzle. Send the exact part number and we confirm the fit before you order.
What is the minimum order and lead time?
We supply from a single replacement piece to a full production batch. The standard nozzle family carries a documented one-day spare-parts lead time; custom or LED tips follow the quoted schedule after the design step.
Can you make a nozzle that is not in the list?
Yes. The documented five-day design service starts from a photograph, not a drawing. Send the part, a handful of them, and the board, plus your daily volume, and we return a nozzle concept — geometry, bore, material, matrix code and head interface.
Ceramic, metal or rubber-pad — which should I choose?
It depends on the component and your wear pattern. Ceramic suits fine-pitch 0201/0402/0603 with low static and long life; metal suits larger, tougher parts; the rubber-pad (G) variants suit sensitive bodies and LEDs that a hard tip would mark. Tell us what you place and we will recommend.
How do I find my nozzle part number?
The FUJI P/N is usually laser-marked on the nozzle body (for example a FU-AAxxxx NXT prefix) or listed in your spares register, and the tip diameter (ø0.7, ø1.3, ø2.5 …) is printed on the flange. If it is worn off, a clear photo of the tip and the head model is enough for us to cross-reference.
Do you supply nozzles for other mounters?
Yes. The same capability covers Yamaha, JUKI, Panasonic NPM, ASM / Siemens and Hitachi nozzles, plus fully customised gripper and vacuum tips. Ask about the brands your line runs.
How do I get more life out of a nozzle?
Keep the vacuum channel clean, change the NXT head filters on schedule, and track cycle counts. Swap on a plan from a named part number rather than waiting for a reject spike, and pair the nozzles with an automatic nozzle cleaner to recover suction.
How do I get a quote?
Email info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576 with the machine model, head position and nozzle part number (or a photo). We reply with a matched part, price and lead time, usually the same working day.
